<reason>Both sides executed well, but B (PRO) built the cleaner path to victory. B's pressure question exposing the prediction contradiction — CON must claim researchers can foresee pandemic potential to justify building, yet claims regulators cannot foresee it to prohibit — was the debate's decisive weapon, and B reinforced it in Rebuttal 2 and the closing. A's answer (a research hypothesis under containment differs from a criminal-standard verdict before any result) is genuinely good and survives, but A repeats it rather than deepening it, and B's rejoinder (if potential is unclear, the "preparation" is rolling dice with a civilizational hazard) lands. B also controlled scope well: every working tool (platform vaccines, surveillance, modeling, work on existing pathogens) stays legal, attacking A's uniqueness claim, while A's best uniqueness answer — mammalian-adaptation markers from constructed changes — was never directly refuted but was outweighed by B's asymmetry frame: speculative, replaceable gain versus demonstrated lab-escape failure mode with no ceiling. A was rhetorically superior ("a computer does not cough," "empty freezer bought with exponential spread") and forced a real scope concession when B admitted a single spike swap counts. B's clipped opening is a minor execution cost, but B answered both pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 structure and crystallized the clash more decisively. Competitive but clear edge to B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.2): turning A's own justification against the undrawability argument — "they cannot claim the prediction is impossible when it's the premise of their entire case" — plus the closing's sharpened version ("if it isn't clear, no one is being prepared; they are rolling dice"). A's hypothesis-versus-verdict reply was its best moment, but B's rejoinder left the contradiction standing as the round's controlling clash.</best_rebuttal>
